contributions.title: Administrative cleanup may leave hospital and drug price power untouched
contributions.body: Administrative simplification may remove billing friction without materially changing hospital pricing leverage, specialist market concentration, or pharmaceutical pricing power. If those cost centers remain intact, the card should not imply that workflow reform alone can bend the total system cost curve very far.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a durable objection to the card's savings thesis. The contribution argues that administrative reform may lower friction while leaving the largest pricing levers outside the proposal's reach.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Keep visible against any claim that simplification alone solves overall cost inflation.

providers.summary: This is a clean objection-lane contribution because it forces the card to separate workflow waste from market power. It should attach to the main cost-savings claim rather than being treated as a side comment.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
providers.reviewerNote: Good pressure against overclaiming total-cost impact.

providers.summary: The strongest feature of this contribution is that it targets the proposal's likely overreach rather than its weakest form. Savings may be real but still strategically insufficient if concentrated price power remains untouched.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
providers.reviewerNote: Preserve as a live objection unless the topic card directly answers the price-power problem.

review.assignedToLabel: Administrative simplification may not resolve hospital or pharmaceutical price leverage
review.decisionReason: Accepted into the objection lane so the card does not overclaim cost relief from administrative reform alone.
review.reviewerNote: Keep tied to the main thesis until the room has a stronger answer on hospitals, specialist networks, and pharmaceuticals.

contributions.title: Administrative overhead is materially significant and worth a direct pilot
contributions.body: A serious evidence contribution should keep the room anchored to the possibility that administrative overhead is large enough to justify focused testing. If a meaningful share of healthcare spending and clinician time is consumed by claims handling, prior authorization, and documentation churn, the card is right to treat simplification as a non-trivial reform lever.

evidenceSource.label: Health Affairs: Slowing the growth of health care spending

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as evidence supporting the claim that administrative overhead is large enough to justify direct testing. Both assisted readers treat it as a strengthening input rather than as a conclusive proof of savings.
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Use as baseline support while keeping the evidence burden high on measured savings.

providers.summary: This contribution strengthens the card's starting claim that paperwork burden is not trivial noise. It belongs in the evidence layer because it justifies testing the topic rather than proving the full proposal.
providers.reviewerNote: Good evidence anchor for why the topic is worth examining.

providers.summary: The contribution is useful because it narrows the claim: administrative burden may be large enough to matter, but the room still has to show where savings are real, durable, and clinically meaningful.
providers.reviewerNote: Keep as support for the room's evidence layer, not as license for overclaiming.

review.decisionReason: Incorporated into the evidence layer because it strengthens the case that administrative waste is large enough to test directly.
review.reviewerNote: Use this as a baseline reference, but continue separating insurer overhead from provider workflow waste.

contributions.title: Transition costs may consume the first years of projected savings
contributions.body: Even if the steady-state model is cleaner, early savings may be consumed by software migration, retraining, contract rewrites, temporary dual workflows, and local implementation failure. The card should pressure-test whether the proposal's timing assumptions are realistic rather than counting gross administrative savings as if the transition were free.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as an economic assumption challenge focused on timing rather than direction. The contribution argues that implementation friction could consume the first wave of nominal savings.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Strong enough to hold open, but still needs quantified transition modeling.

providers.summary: The contribution is important because many reform models confuse long-run plausibility with near-term fiscal credibility. Early implementation drag may determine whether the reform is survivable at all.
providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings
providers.reviewerNote: Treat as a real stress test on the card's economic optimism.

review.assignedToLabel: Transition costs stay below early administrative savings

contributions.title: AI triage helps only if human-escalation thresholds are explicit
contributions.body: AI-assisted triage may be genuinely useful for routine routing, intake normalization, and low-risk redirection. But the card should treat it as bounded support, not autonomous judgment. Hard human-escalation thresholds, override ownership, and auditability need to be part of the design or the triage layer becomes a new clinical risk instead of a workflow improvement.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as nuance with implementation implications. The contribution narrows the AI claim by requiring explicit escalation thresholds and human override design.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Useful because it improves the card without collapsing into generic anti-AI skepticism.

providers.suggestedAssignmentLabel: AI triage is safe only if escalation thresholds and human override paths are explicit
providers.reviewerNote: Good narrowing move that makes the topic more governable.

providers.summary: The strength of this contribution is that it rescues the proposal from vague automation optimism. It identifies the boundary condition that determines whether AI triage is a support layer or a liability generator.

contributions.title: Paperwork reduction matters only if time actually returns to care teams
contributions.body: A provider-facing perspective should ask whether reduced clicks, fewer forms, or faster intake actually give time back to nurses, physicians, and coordinators. If reclaimed minutes are immediately reabsorbed into new compliance tasks or higher throughput demands, the card may mistake administrative rearrangement for real clinical relief.

aiIntake.summary: Sorted as a personal/provider perspective with measurable operational implications. The contribution argues that savings claims should be tested against time actually returned to care teams.
aiIntake.suggestedAssignmentLabel: How should the room measure whether simplification returns time to clinical care rather than to new compliance demands?
aiIntake.reviewerNote: Good contribution, but it needs a sharper measurement frame before it can move the card.
